passage:
The history of jazz piano has long been narrated as a story of progressive liberation: from the metronomic regularity of ragtime, through the loping stride style of Harlem's ballroom masters, and finally toward the harmonically daring improvisation that came to define bebop in the 1940s. Within this familiar arc, Thelonious Monk occupies a peculiar position — praised almost universally, yet rarely placed with confidence within any of its phases. Standard accounts tend to celebrate Monk as a visionary whose angular melodies and deliberately dissonant chord voicings anticipated the harmonic freedoms that later pianists exploited. The truth, however, is more complicated: Monk was not so much a prophet of what came after him as a renovator of what had come before.

The case for Monk as a forward-looking modernist rests largely on the surface strangeness of his playing. His use of clustered, unresolved chord voicings, his habit of striking notes and then withdrawing into silence while the rhythm section continued, and his willfully awkward phrasing struck many contemporary listeners as wilfully eccentric. Yet these very qualities, on closer inspection, reveal a deep engagement with the older vocabulary of stride piano. Monk's left hand, often dismissed as merely erratic, in fact traces the fundamental stride pattern — the alternating bass note and mid-register chord — at irregular, syncopated intervals, a deliberate deformation of the tradition rather than a departure from it. His silences, too, are not absences of ideas but rather spaces that make the stride architecture beneath them audible by contrast. Where later bebop pianists crowded their lines with chromatic runs, Monk subtracted.

What makes this interpretive tension productive is that Monk's renovation of stride was never merely nostalgic. He subjected the conventions of the tradition to an ironic pressure — elongating phrases just past the point of comfortable resolution, voicing chords in ways that simultaneously honored their functional harmonic role and exposed its arbitrariness. The effect, to borrow a phrase from one mid-century critic, was of "familiar furniture rearranged in a dark room": the listener sensed the known shapes but could not quite settle into them. This quality gave Monk's music a dual audience — it was legible to dancers and listeners trained on the Harlem stride tradition, and it was simultaneously fascinating to younger musicians searching for ways to press beyond conventional harmony. But Monk himself, by all biographical evidence, was indifferent to which audience claimed him. His primary loyalty was to the internal logic of each composition, to the feeling he described, in his characteristically laconic manner, as "making the music sound the way it is."

The tendency to read Monk's work primarily through the lens of what came after — to treat him as a way station on the road to free jazz — impoverishes our understanding of his achievement. His greatness lay not in anticipation but in compression: in the ability to hold within a single performance the stride tradition's rhythmic authority, the bebop era's harmonic restlessness, and a quality of structural irony that belonged to neither movement and to both.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thelonious Monk's piano technique was primarily derived from the bebop movement's emphasis on chromatic improvisation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Standard accounts of jazz history have underestimated the influence of the Harlem stride tradition on the development of bebop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monk's achievement is best understood not as a harbinger of later jazz developments but as an ironic renovation of the stride tradition he inherited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monk's music appealed to two distinct audiences because he deliberately balanced accessibility with harmonic experimentation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The silences in Monk's playing constitute his most original contribution to jazz piano, distinguishing him from both stride and bebop practitioners.

explanations.correct: The passage argues across all four paragraphs that Monk is better understood as a renovator of stride than as a prophet of what came after — this is the thesis introduced at the end of paragraph 1 and substantiated throughout.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly argues against treating Monk as a bebop figure; bebop pianists are contrasted with Monk's subtractive approach.
explanations.B: This is a related point, but the passage's argument centers on Monk specifically, not on the broader underestimation of stride's influence on bebop generally.
explanations.C: Correct. This integrates the thesis from paragraph 1 ('renovator of what had come before') with the irony argument of paragraphs 3 and 4.
explanations.D: The dual-audience point appears in paragraph 3 but is a supporting detail, not the main thesis; the passage also notes Monk was indifferent to which audience claimed him.
explanations.E: The silence observation appears in paragraph 2 as one piece of evidence for the broader claim; treating it as Monk's 'most original contribution' overstates its role and misrepresents the thesis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard account of Monk as a visionary who anticipated later harmonic freedoms can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete rejection, on the grounds that it misidentifies Monk's primary musical influences

choices.label: B
choices.text: partial acceptance, since the account captures Monk's surface strangeness while missing the deeper sources of his originality

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, because Monk's dissonant voicings did in fact shape the bebop pianists who followed him

choices.label: D
choices.text: measured skepticism, since the account applies to some of Monk's recordings but not to his most representative work

choices.label: E
choices.text: indifference, because the author considers questions of historical influence less important than questions of compositional logic

explanations.correct: The author does not deny that Monk sounded strange or unconventional — those surface qualities are acknowledged — but argues that the standard account mistakes the origin and character of that strangeness, attributing it to forward-looking modernism when it actually derives from a renovated stride tradition.
explanations.A: Too strong; the author does not fully reject the standard account but complicates it by pointing to what it misses. The phrase 'the truth is more complicated' signals partial, not total, disagreement.
explanations.B: Correct. The passage concedes the 'surface strangeness' reading has some basis ('the case for Monk as a forward-looking modernist rests largely on the surface strangeness of his playing') but argues it fails to reach the deeper stride-renovation story.
explanations.C: The opposite of the author's stance; the author specifically resists reading Monk through the lens of what came after.
explanations.D: The author makes no distinction among different recordings or phases of Monk's career; the argument applies to his work generally.
explanations.E: The author clearly cares about historical placement — the entire passage is an argument about where in jazz history Monk belongs — making indifference implausible.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biographical sketch of a musician is offered, followed by an account of his stylistic evolution, and then a defense of his place in the jazz canon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A standard interpretive view is introduced, evidence for a rival view is presented, the rival view is enriched by a further qualification, and the standard view's inadequacy is restated as a conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing critical frameworks for evaluating a musician's work are described, a third framework is proposed, and the three are reconciled in the final paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A claim about a musician's historical influence is made, qualified by biographical evidence, and then extended to cover the broader development of jazz as a genre.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A widely-held view is endorsed, its strongest counterargument is presented, and the original view is ultimately reaffirmed with minor concessions.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the standard 'forward-looking visionary' account; paragraph 2 marshals evidence that Monk was actually renovating stride; paragraph 3 qualifies that renovation as ironic rather than nostalgic; paragraph 4 restates the inadequacy of reading Monk through what came after. This matches choice B exactly.
explanations.A: The passage is not biographical and does not trace a stylistic evolution across Monk's career; it makes an interpretive argument about the nature of his achievement.
explanations.B: Correct. Each paragraph corresponds precisely: standard view (¶1), rival evidence (¶2), qualification (¶3), restatement of the standard view's inadequacy (¶4).
explanations.C: Only two interpretive frames are explicitly in tension (the modernist/bebop reading and the stride-renovation reading); no third framework is proposed.
explanations.D: Biographical evidence plays a minor role (Monk's own comment in ¶3) and is not the main vehicle of the argument; the passage does not broaden to cover jazz development generally.
explanations.E: The passage does not ultimately reaffirm the standard view; it replaces it with the author's rival reading.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following characterizes the stride piano technique that Monk employed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A continuous chromatic run in the left hand that anchored the melody played by the right hand

choices.label: B
choices.text: An alternating pattern of bass notes and mid-register chords in the left hand

choices.label: C
choices.text: A metronomic, highly regular pulse maintained throughout each performance

choices.label: D
choices.text: A preference for unresolved dissonances that exposed the arbitrariness of conventional harmonic function

choices.label: E
choices.text: A series of silences that made the structural logic of each composition audible by contrast

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that the stride pattern involves 'the alternating bass note and mid-register chord' in the left hand. Monk traces this pattern, though at irregular intervals.
explanations.A: Chromatic runs are attributed to bebop pianists ('later bebop pianists crowded their lines with chromatic runs'), not to the stride tradition.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the verbatim description of stride in paragraph 2.
explanations.C: Metronomic regularity is attributed to ragtime in paragraph 1, not to stride.
explanations.D: The exposure of harmonic arbitrariness is attributed to Monk's ironic renovation of stride in paragraph 3, not to stride itself.
explanations.E: The strategic use of silences is described as Monk's own practice — his deformation of stride — not as a feature of the stride tradition per se.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of bebop pianists of the 1940s?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were directly influenced by Monk's use of stride architecture and strategic silence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their approach to harmonic improvisation differed from Monk's in that they favored adding rather than subtracting musical material.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They regarded the stride tradition as an inferior predecessor that had to be entirely rejected before genuine innovation was possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They were more concerned with compositional structure than with the emotional effect of individual performances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their work appealed primarily to younger musicians rather than to audiences trained in the stride tradition.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that 'later bebop pianists crowded their lines with chromatic runs,' while Monk 'subtracted.' The contrast implies bebop pianists added material where Monk removed it — a difference of additive versus subtractive approaches to harmonic elaboration.
explanations.A: The passage makes no claim that bebop pianists were influenced by Monk's specific techniques; the causal relationship runs the other way in the standard account (Monk anticipated them), and the author disputes even that framing.
explanations.B: Correct. The explicit contrast between bebop pianists who 'crowded their lines' and Monk who 'subtracted' supports this inference directly.
explanations.C: The passage does not characterize bebop pianists' attitude toward stride; this inference goes beyond what the passage supports.
explanations.D: No claim about bebop pianists' priorities regarding structure versus emotional effect appears in the passage.
explanations.E: The dual-audience observation in paragraph 3 applies to Monk's music, not to bebop pianists generally.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely quotes the mid-century critic's phrase "familiar furniture rearranged in a dark room" (third paragraph) primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide documentary evidence that Monk's contemporaries recognized his debt to the stride tradition

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate the quality of disoriented familiarity produced by Monk's ironic treatment of conventional harmonic structures

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast Monk's reception among critics with his reception among dancers and younger musicians

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that Monk's music was ultimately more accessible than it appeared to first-time listeners

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce the biographical evidence that Monk was indifferent to audience expectations

explanations.correct: The critic's phrase is cited immediately after the author describes Monk's practice of 'simultaneously honoring' harmonic convention and 'exposing its arbitrariness.' The furniture metaphor captures exactly that double quality — the listener recognizes familiar shapes but cannot settle into them — and thus illustrates the ironic pressure Monk applied to stride conventions.
explanations.A: The critic's phrase does not address Monk's stride debt; it addresses the listener's experience of his harmonic practice. Using it as documentary evidence of the stride connection would be a misapplication.
explanations.B: Correct. The phrase functions to make the abstract claim about 'ironic pressure' and 'familiar yet disorienting' harmony concrete and vivid.
explanations.C: The dual-audience contrast appears later in the same paragraph and is not the purpose of the critic's phrase.
explanations.D: The passage does not argue that Monk was more accessible than he seemed; the furniture metaphor suggests lingering disorientation, not resolved accessibility.
explanations.E: Monk's biographical indifference is introduced in the following sentence, after the critic's phrase; the phrase does not introduce it.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle the author describes as characteristic of Monk's relationship to the stride tradition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist abandons the epistolary format of eighteenth-century fiction entirely and invents a radically new narrative structure with no debt to its predecessors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A choreographer employs the vocabulary of classical ballet — its positions, its vocabulary of steps — but introduces irregular rhythms and unexpected pauses that make the underlying structure visible as structure rather than as invisible convention.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A filmmaker borrows the visual iconography of the Western genre in order to satirize the political assumptions that genre has historically reinforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A poet translates a medieval text into contemporary idiom, preserving the original's imagery while substituting modern syntax and diction throughout.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A jazz saxophonist studies the recordings of earlier masters in order to reproduce their style as faithfully as possible in live performance.

explanations.correct: The author characterizes Monk's relationship to stride as a 'deliberate deformation' rather than departure — retaining the tradition's architecture while subjecting it to ironic pressure that makes its conventions visible and strange. The choreographer in B retains classical ballet's vocabulary but deforms it through irregular rhythms and unexpected pauses, making the underlying structure 'visible as structure rather than as invisible convention.' This matches the mechanism precisely.
explanations.A: This describes wholesale rejection of a prior tradition, the opposite of what the author attributes to Monk, who retained stride's architecture rather than abandoning it.
explanations.B: Correct. Retaining the inherited vocabulary while deforming its rhythmic regularity to expose the underlying structure mirrors Monk's stride renovation exactly.
explanations.C: Satire involves using a form to critique its own assumptions, which is closer to parody — and the passage explicitly distinguishes Monk's project from parody in paragraphs 1 and 3.
explanations.D: Faithful translation of imagery while changing syntax describes adaptation, not the ironic pressure that makes familiar conventions feel both recognized and disorienting.
explanations.E: Faithful reproduction of an earlier style describes imitation without deformation, which is the opposite of Monk's approach as the author describes it.
